newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia trade sees USDA figures as bearish.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia trade sees USDA figures as bearish.

text.p: Solid falls in wheat futures in Chicago and Sydney in reaction to growing USDA crop forecast figures have set the tone for a continuing decline in world grain prices, Australian traders and analysts mostly believe.
The threat of a subsidy war between Europe and the U.S. is also seen as adding to downward pressure on prices.
The prevailing Australian view is that wheat prices will continue to fall for the foreseeable future in reaction to a USDA grain crop forecast which has now come to grips with a big world harvest.

Colin Lethbridge of ANZ McCaughan Futures Ltd, a partly dissenting voice, said he was surprised by the market reaction to the USDA figures and was still not convinced the forecast heralds much lower prices in the short-term.
But Lethbridge and the bears of the Australian market base differing conclusions on ultimately common ground.

"Even though the world is going to have the fourth largest crop in history, that will satisfy demand (only) in the very short-term," Lethbridge said. "If there is any production glitch around the world, prices will go spiralling again because it doesn't add to the world stocks," he said. "
Phil Lindsay of Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures Ltd saw wheat prices drifting down for months but also said the underlying problem of tight stocks remained.
Lindsay saw the January Sydney Futures Exchange (SFE) Australian Standard White (ASW) wheat contract drifting toward A$165 from its Thursday sale of A$177.
With worldwide consumption of grain still accelerating, the bumper world crop would not rectify a fundamentally tight market but only temporarily shift it toward supply, he said.
The global stocks-to-use ratio the second lowest in USDA's database, which began in 1960/61, he said.

Ben Suttie of C A & L Bell Commodities Corp Pty Ltd said the USDA report was negative for wheat, with the carryover increased to 506 million bushels, up by nearly 100 million bushels on the August forecast of 409 million. "Wheat looks easier," he said.

John Ricketts of Perth Commodities and Futures Brokers Pty Ltd said he expected the Chicago December wheat price to fall to US$4.25 a bushel from the present $4.40, but then bounce to about $5.20 or so by next March.
The turnaround in sentiment in the last three months had been incredible, he said.
In May this year world wheat crops were seen as heading toward disaster, but now a 580 million tonne world crop was huge, he said.
"It's nothing like the disaster we were looking at in May."
Australian traders believe that the USDA has its latest forecast, of a 579.50 million tonne world wheat crop for 1996/97 against 535.93 million, mostly right.
This, as Ricketts said, was a reversal of figures in the previous month when production was played down.

The USDA was only confirming what the market had known for the past three weeks, Lindsay said. Still, the world was slowly coming to the realisation that world wheat prices would remain soft for the remainder of the year, he said.
The USDA estimate of a 19.5 million tonne Australian wheat crop for 1996/97, however, is seen as conservative.
"Ord Minnett is still looking for 20-22 million tonnes," Lindsay said.
A looming interplay between threatened EU-U.S. subsidy warfare and the failure of the world's biggest wheat buyers to enter the market is seen as a further weight on the market.
With France already subsidising its wheat, U.S. subsidies may become an important factor, Suttie said.
"If it develops any further into a bit of a trade war, you'd expect the U.S. to come out to use (funds allocated for) subsidy," he said.
If quality buyers did not enter the market soon there would be pressure on the USDA from U.S. exporters to act, he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
